entries.note:
The `accepts` callback is the whole reason this layer can serve both a window and a headset, and it is the part a later editor is most likely to 'simplify' back into a surface check.

Selecting a physical device needs a question this layer cannot ask. The desktop's question is "can this queue family present to my surface" — which needs a VkSurfaceKHR, and creating one here would make the layer useless to OpenXR, where there is no surface at all and the runtime instead names the adapter its headset is on. So the layer enumerates and filters on what is universal (API 1.3, dynamic rendering, synchronization2, shader demote, the caller's extensions) and hands each candidate to the host.

The desktop's callback creates its surface on the first call, because that is the only moment it can: the surface needs the instance, and the instance is created inside re_gpu_open. Windowing therefore lives in backend_vk.c where it belongs, and tools/design.py's native_gpu_device_layer gate fails the build if a surface, swapchain, present or SDL symbol appears here.

Verified on this machine after all. It was recorded as unrunnable here (KI-079) because SDL answered "Failed to load Vulkan Portability library" — but Homebrew's molten-vk and vulkan-loader were already installed, and only the ICD manifest was missing from the loader's search path (it lives under etc/, not share/). With VK_ICD_FILENAMES set, this file runs against MoltenVK on an M3 Max and the Vulkan backend matches the SDL reference on every scene with zero validation messages. It was still written as a move of backend_vk.c's creation code rather than a rewrite, which is why the diff was reviewable.

The parts a single-GPU machine cannot reach — two queue families, a predicate that refuses, a device below the feature floor — are covered by tests/gpu_device_test.c, which supplies its own vkGetInstanceProcAddr.
